output.title: Decreasing students’ stress through time management training

scenes.narration: University students often feel stressed, and this paper asks whether a short time management training can change that in higher education.
scenes.layout_description: A student sits at a desk surrounded by papers, with a small clock and an orange arrow pointing toward a calmer posture.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal hand-drawn student at cluttered desk, clock nearby, stress lines around head, then a simple orange arrow toward a tidier desk and relaxed shoulders.

scenes.narration: The authors studied twenty-three undergraduate students who joined a training and reported demands, perceived stress, and perceived control of time before and after it.
scenes.layout_description: Three labeled boxes show the same students at three moments, with arrows moving from left to right.
scenes.visual_prompt: Three-panel sketch of the same student group at pretest, 2 weeks, and 4 weeks, with simple icons for demands, tension, and control.

scenes.narration: They used a non-equivalent dependent variable design, meaning one variable should change with training, while demands should stay unchanged as a comparison.
scenes.layout_description: A balance-like drawing shows two expected-changing variables on one side and demands on the other, with the demands side steady.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple scale illustration: one side has stress and control icons, the other has a demands stack held steady by a fixed weight.

scenes.narration: The training focused on prioritizing, goal setting, strategy development, daily planning, and monitoring, all meant to help students manage time better.
scenes.layout_description: Five small icons are arranged in a row, each linked by orange arrows to show the training flow.
scenes.visual_prompt: A sequence of hand-drawn icons: list, target, stepping stones, calendar, checklist, all connected by orange arrows.

scenes.narration: Students reflected on their activities, set concrete and challenging goals, planned steps, and thought about obstacles and deadlines.
scenes.layout_description: A student writes on a sheet with a target, a path, and small rocks representing obstacles.
scenes.visual_prompt: Student at table drawing a path toward a target, with small obstacle stones and a deadline flag.

scenes.narration: They also made daily schedules and monitored task completion, because the authors thought these strategies could reduce stress and increase control of time.
scenes.layout_description: A calendar page and checklist sit beside a clock, with orange circles highlighting completed tasks.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal calendar with checked boxes, a clock, and a calm student pointing to completed tasks.

scenes.narration: The sample came from a medium-sized German university, and students from all faculties were invited as an extracurricular activity.
scenes.layout_description: A simple campus building with students from different subjects walking toward one room.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn university building with diverse student figures carrying books, moving toward a training room.

scenes.narration: The training lasted 4 h, and the researchers measured outcomes directly before training, then 2 weeks later, and again 4 weeks later.
scenes.layout_description: A horizontal timeline shows three measurement points with a small clock above the training block.
scenes.visual_prompt: Timeline with a training block in the middle and three marked points, using orange dots for the measurement times.

scenes.narration: Of the forty-eight students who started, twenty-three completed all questionnaires, and those twenty-three were used for the main analyses.
scenes.layout_description: A funnel-like drawing narrows from forty-eight figures to twenty-three figures at the bottom.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple participant flow sketch: many small student icons narrowing to a smaller group, with the final group highlighted in orange.

scenes.narration: The final group had a mean age of 23.30 years, and 52 % were female, with students from several different subjects.
scenes.layout_description: A cluster of student icons is surrounded by small subject symbols and a few gender markers.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal group portrait of students with varied books and subject symbols, one orange circle marking the 52 % note.

scenes.narration: Before training, many students reported little or no experience with time management strategies, which the authors later discuss as important.
scenes.layout_description: A student looks at a small ladder labeled with experience levels, with the lower rungs emphasized.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn student beside a simple experience ladder, with the lower steps highlighted in yellow.

scenes.narration: Time management behaviour was measured with eighteen items, perceived stress with the tension scale, perceived control of time with ten items, and demands with five items.
scenes.layout_description: Four small measurement cards are lined up, each with a tiny icon and a number.
scenes.visual_prompt: Four paper cards on a table, each showing a simple icon for behavior, tension, control, and demands, with the item counts handwritten.

scenes.narration: At time 1, time management behaviour related positively to perceived control of time, and perceived control of time related negatively to stress and demands.
scenes.layout_description: Three arrows connect the variables, with orange arrows showing the direction of the relationships.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple network diagram with circles for behavior, control, stress, and demands, using arrows and one highlighted negative link.

scenes.narration: After training, trainees reported more frequent use of the taught strategies, with a significant increase by 4 weeks and a nearly significant increase by 2 weeks.
scenes.layout_description: A checklist grows fuller across two later time points, with the later point emphasized in orange.
scenes.visual_prompt: Three small checklists in sequence, each more filled in, with the last one circled in orange and the middle one marked as nearly significant.

scenes.narration: For perceived stress, the repeated-measures analysis showed a significant overall time effect and a significant effect at 2 weeks after training.
scenes.layout_description: A line graph for stress slopes downward from pretest to the first posttest, with the drop highlighted.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal line graph with a downward stress line, orange highlight on the first drop, and a small star near significance.

scenes.narration: At 2 weeks, trainees reported significantly less stress than before training, while perceived control of time only showed a tendency in the expected direction.
scenes.layout_description: Two side-by-side icons show a lowered stress gauge and a control gauge moving upward only slightly.
scenes.visual_prompt: Split illustration: left a stress meter dropping, right a control meter rising a little, with a small orange note for tendency.

scenes.narration: By 4 weeks, both outcomes changed significantly: perceived stress was lower, and perceived control of time was higher than before training.
scenes.layout_description: Two arrows point in opposite directions from the pretest to the final posttest, one down for stress and one up for control.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple two-line graph, one descending and one ascending, both ending with orange highlights at the 4-week point.

scenes.narration: The control variable, demands, did not change significantly at either posttest, which supported the authors' design logic.
scenes.layout_description: A steady line for demands stays flat across all three time points, unlike the other variables.
scenes.visual_prompt: Flat line graph labeled demands, with three equal points and no upward or downward movement.

scenes.narration: The authors say the effects were stronger for students with no or little experience, especially for perceived stress, than for those with more experience.
scenes.layout_description: Two student groups stand side by side, with the less experienced group surrounded by larger orange effect circles.
scenes.visual_prompt: Two clusters of students, one with bigger orange arrows showing stronger change, the other with smaller arrows.

scenes.narration: In discussion, the authors argue that prioritizing, goal setting, daily planning, and monitoring may have given students more orientation and control.
scenes.layout_description: A path, a calendar, and a checklist are arranged like stepping stones toward a target.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn path toward a target, with calendar and checklist icons acting as stepping stones, highlighted in orange.

scenes.narration: They also note that the training was short, only 4 h, yet it still had a positive impact in a mixed student sample.
scenes.layout_description: A small clock sits beside a group of students, showing that the intervention was brief but effective.
scenes.visual_prompt: Clock next to a small group of students with a gentle upward arrow and calm faces.

scenes.narration: The authors caution that the sample was small and that more studies with larger student samples are needed for stronger conclusions.
scenes.layout_description: A tiny sample jar sits beside a larger empty outline, suggesting the need for more participants.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal sketch of a small group of students beside a much larger faint outline group, with an orange question mark.

scenes.narration: They also mention that about half the students left before the second measurement, although they say such dropout rates are common.
scenes.layout_description: A group of students splits, with some walking away from the timeline before the second point.
scenes.visual_prompt: Participant flow drawing showing several figures leaving a timeline, while the remaining group stays highlighted.

scenes.narration: The paper suggests comparing time management training with other stress-reducing interventions, and also testing whether effects last and whether performance changes.
scenes.layout_description: Three small boxes show training, a clock, and a grade sheet, linked by orange arrows.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal comparison scene with a training icon, a long-lasting clock, and a performance paper, all connected by arrows.

scenes.narration: For students, the authors suggest prioritizing tasks, setting clear goals with deadlines, planning the work day, and monitoring progress.
scenes.layout_description: A student checklist is shown beside a calendar and a target, all neatly arranged.
scenes.visual_prompt: Student holding a checklist next to a calendar with deadline marks and a target, in clean line art.

scenes.narration: They also suggest that universities could teach these strategies in freshman programs or in courses with long projects or exam preparation.
scenes.layout_description: A university classroom scene shows a teacher pointing to a calendar and project sheet.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple classroom with a lecturer, students, a project paper, and an exam calendar on the board.

scenes.narration: Overall, the study suggests time management training may help undergraduate students feel less stressed and more in control of their time.
scenes.layout_description: The final image brings together a calm student, a clock, and a checklist in a balanced composition.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal closing illustration of a relaxed student beside a clock and checklist, with orange and yellow accents showing calm control.
